tools.name: configuration_view
tools.description: Get the current Kubernetes configuration content as a kubeconfig YAML

minified.description: Return a minified version of the configuration. If set to true, keeps only the current-context and the relevant pieces of the configuration for that context. If set to false, all contexts, clusters, auth-infos, and users are returned in the configuration. (Optional, default true)

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: helm_install
tools.description: Install (deploy) a Helm chart to create a release in the current or provided namespace

chart.description: Chart reference to install (for example: stable/grafana, oci://ghcr.io/nginxinc/charts/nginx-ingress)

name.description: Name of the Helm release (Optional, random name if not provided)

namespace.description: Namespace to install the Helm chart in (Optional, current namespace if not provided)

values.description: Values to pass to the Helm chart (Optional)

tools.description: List all the Helm releases in the current or provided namespace (or in all namespaces if specified)

name.description: Name of the Helm release to uninstall

namespace.description: Namespace to uninstall the Helm release from (Optional, current namespace if not provided)

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

Done.

What I applied:
- Deployed canary Deployment engine-v2-1 (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - replicas: 2
  - labels: app: recommendation-engine, version: v2.1
  - container: rec-engine
    - containerPort: 80 (matches stable)
  - pod securityContext: {} (matches stable)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1
  - port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080 preserved

Traffic split:
- With 2 pods in engine-v2-0 and 2 pods in engine-v2-1 behind the same Service, Kubernetes will distribute roughly evenly across endpoints, yielding ~50/50 canary vs stable.

If you want me to, I can verify the canary rollout status and endpoints selected by the Service. 
To fine-tune the split, scale either deployment (e.g., 3:1 for ~75/25). To roll back, either scale the canary to 0 or revert the Service selector to include version=v2.0 only.

deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

What I applied:

  - image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - replicas: 2
  - labels: app: recommendation-engine, version: v2.1
  - container: rec-engine
    - containerPort: 80 (matches stable)
  - pod securityContext: {} (matches stable)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine (namespace canary-deployment-ns)
  - selector changed from app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1
  - port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080 preserved

Traffic split:
- With 2 pods in engine-v2-0 and 2 pods in engine-v2-1 behind the same Service, Kubernetes will distribute roughly evenly across endpoints, yielding ~50/50 canary vs stable.

If you want me to, I can verify the canary rollout status and endpoints selected by the Service. 
To fine-tune the split, scale either deployment (e.g., 3:1 for ~75/25). To roll back, either scale the canary to 0 or revert the Service selector to include version=v2.0 only.

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

What was wrong
- The Deployment’s container was started with: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, causing CrashLoopBackOff.

What I changed
- Recreated the Deployment without the invalid command so the nginx image uses its default startup.
- Kept image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged and set containerPort: 8080.

Current status
- Pod is healthy: app-6df8647c78-xh77r in crashloop-test is 1/1 Running, 0 restarts.

Want me to expose it via a Service or Ingress/Route?

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) specified storageClassName=sc, but no such StorageClass existed.

What I changed
- Created a StorageClass named sc that uses the existing local-path provisioner (rancher.io/local-path), reclaimPolicy=Delete, volumeBindingMode=WaitForFirstConsumer.

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound
- PV: dynamically provisioned and bound to the PVC
- Pod homepage-pod: Running on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane (Pod IP: 10.244.0.30)

If you’d prefer to use the default StorageClass (“standard”) instead of creating “sc,” I can update your manifests for future deployments and remove the extra StorageClass—just say the word.

namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) specified storageClassName=sc, but no such StorageClass existed.

What I changed
- Created a StorageClass named sc that uses the existing local-path provisioner (rancher.io/local-path), reclaimPolicy=Delete, volumeBindingMode=WaitForFirstConsumer.

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound
- PV: dynamically provisioned and bound to the PVC
- Pod homepage-pod: Running on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane (Pod IP: 10.244.0.30)

If you’d prefer to use the default StorageClass (“standard”) instead of creating “sc,” I can update your manifests for future deployments and remove the extra StorageClass—just say the word.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) specified storageClassName=sc, but no such StorageClass existed.

What I changed
- Created a StorageClass named sc that uses the existing local-path provisioner (rancher.io/local-path), reclaimPolicy=Delete, volumeBindingMode=WaitForFirstConsumer.

Current state
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound
- PV: dynamically provisioned and bound to the PVC
- Pod homepage-pod: Running on node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane (Pod IP: 10.244.0.30)

If you’d prefer to use the default StorageClass (“standard”) instead of creating “sc,” I can update your manifests for future deployments and remove the extra StorageClass—just say the word.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The Deployment’s health probes were pointing to non-existent endpoints on the wrong port:
  - Liveness: GET /get_status on port 80
  - Readiness: GET /is_ready on port 80

I found and fixed the issue.

Root cause
- The Deployment’s health probes were pointing to non-existent endpoints on the wrong port:
  - Liveness: GET /get_status on port 80
  - Readiness: GET /is_ready on port 80
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080 by default, not 80.
- The Service was also targeting container port 80, so traffic couldn’t reach the app.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment’s probes to use GET / on port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080.

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Ready and Running in the orders namespace.
- Service “webapp” is serving on port 80 -> container 8080.

How to verify quickly
- In-cluster: kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -c 'curl -sS http://webapp'
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080

Root cause
- The Deployment’s health probes were pointing to non-existent endpoints on the wrong port:
  - Liveness: GET /get_status on port 80
  - Readiness: GET /is_ready on port 80
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080 by default, not 80.
- The Service was also targeting container port 80, so traffic couldn’t reach the app.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment’s probes to use GET / on port 8080.
- Updated the Service to targetPort 8080.

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Ready and Running in the orders namespace.
- Service “webapp” is serving on port 80 -> container 8080.

How to verify quickly
- In-cluster: kubectl -n orders run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -c 'curl -sS http://webapp'
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080

Need external access?
- There’s no Ingress configured. I can create an Ingress (or LoadBalancer Service) if you share the desired hostname or exposure method.

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Deployment/Pods label: app=nginx
  - Result: no endpoints, so the Service had nothing to send traffic to.
- The container listens on port 8080, but the Service was targeting port 80.
  - Verified inside the pod: nginx listens on 8080.

Fix applied
- Updated the Service in namespace web:
  - selector changed to app=nginx
  - targetPort changed to 8080 (Service port remains 80)

Verification
- Endpoints now populated for svc/nginx:
  - Pod IP 10.244.0.34 on port 8080
- In-pod test:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local returned “HTTP/1.1 200 OK”
- This confirms the Service is reachable inside the cluster at nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80.

How you can test
- From any pod in the cluster:
  - kubectl -n web exec deploy/nginx -- curl -sSI http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local | head -n1
- From your machine (temporary):
  - kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80
  - curl -I http://localhost:8080

If you need access from outside the cluster
- Option A: NodePort
  - Expose the Service via NodePort and reach it on any node’s IP:nodePort.
- Option B: Ingress (recommended if you have an Ingress controller)
  - Create an Ingress to route HTTP traffic to svc/nginx:80.

Tell me which exposure method you prefer and any hostname you want, and I can set it up.

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pods:
  - Service selector: app=web
  - Deployment/Pods label: app=nginx
  - Result: no endpoints, so the Service had nothing to send traffic to.
- The container listens on port 8080, but the Service was targeting port 80.
  - Verified inside the pod: nginx listens on 8080.

Fix applied
- Updated the Service in namespace web:
  - selector changed to app=nginx
  - targetPort changed to 8080 (Service port remains 80)

Verification
- Endpoints now populated for svc/nginx:
  - Pod IP 10.244.0.34 on port 8080
- In-pod test:
  - curl http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local returned “HTTP/1.1 200 OK”
- This confirms the Service is reachable inside the cluster at nginx.web.svc.cluster.local:80.

How you can test
- From any pod in the cluster:
  - kubectl -n web exec deploy/nginx -- curl -sSI http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local | head -n1
- From your machine (temporary):
  - kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80
  - curl -I http://localhost:8080

If you need access from outside the cluster
- Option A: NodePort
  - Expose the Service via NodePort and reach it on any node’s IP:nodePort.
- Option B: Ingress (recommended if you have an Ingress controller)
  - Create an Ingress to route HTTP traffic to svc/nginx:80.

Tell me which exposure method you prefer and any hostname you want, and I can set it up.

results.taskOutput:
Summary of findings
- Root cause: The web-app pods were Pending due to a nodeSelector that didn’t match any nodes.
  - Deployment had: nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu
  - Your cluster node(s) don’t have that label, so the scheduler couldn’t place the pods.
  - This left the Service with no endpoints, which caused connection refused to web-app-service.

What I changed to fix it
- I removed the mismatching nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it (server-side apply couldn’t remove the field due to field ownership, so I deleted and re-applied).
- Result: pods scheduled on the available node and are now running.

Current state (verified)
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-sp2xc: Running (1/1)
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-zc9sf: Running (1/1)
- Service endpoints for web-app-service now list both pod IPs on port 80, so traffic will route correctly.

Why the error happened
- With no ready pods behind the Service, connecting to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 returned connection refused.

If you intended to pin these pods to special nodes
- Option A: Re-add a nodeSelector that matches real node labels (e.g., environment=production) after labeling the target node(s): kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu
- Option B: Use node affinity with fallbacks or taints/tolerations as appropriate.
- Let me know and I can reapply a placement policy that fits your environment.

Next steps I can do on request
- Add readiness/liveness probes for nginx to improve rollout safety.
- Create a quick test pod in the namespace to curl the Service and confirm end-to-end response content.
- Set resource requests/limits as needed.

For now, the deployment is fixed and serving through the Service.

namespace/webshop-frontend created

Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Summary of findings
- Root cause: The web-app pods were Pending due to a nodeSelector that didn’t match any nodes.
  - Deployment had: nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu
  - Your cluster node(s) don’t have that label, so the scheduler couldn’t place the pods.
  - This left the Service with no endpoints, which caused connection refused to web-app-service.

What I changed to fix it
- I removed the mismatching nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it (server-side apply couldn’t remove the field due to field ownership, so I deleted and re-applied).
- Result: pods scheduled on the available node and are now running.

Current state (verified)
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-sp2xc: Running (1/1)
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-zc9sf: Running (1/1)
- Service endpoints for web-app-service now list both pod IPs on port 80, so traffic will route correctly.

Why the error happened
- With no ready pods behind the Service, connecting to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 returned connection refused.

If you intended to pin these pods to special nodes
- Option A: Re-add a nodeSelector that matches real node labels (e.g., environment=production) after labeling the target node(s): kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu
- Option B: Use node affinity with fallbacks or taints/tolerations as appropriate.
- Let me know and I can reapply a placement policy that fits your environment.

Next steps I can do on request
- Add readiness/liveness probes for nginx to improve rollout safety.
- Create a quick test pod in the namespace to curl the Service and confirm end-to-end response content.
- Set resource requests/limits as needed.

For now, the deployment is fixed and serving through the Service.

outputSteps.content:
Summary of findings
- Root cause: The web-app pods were Pending due to a nodeSelector that didn’t match any nodes.
  - Deployment had: nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu
  - Your cluster node(s) don’t have that label, so the scheduler couldn’t place the pods.
  - This left the Service with no endpoints, which caused connection refused to web-app-service.

What I changed to fix it
- I removed the mismatching nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it (server-side apply couldn’t remove the field due to field ownership, so I deleted and re-applied).
- Result: pods scheduled on the available node and are now running.

Current state (verified)
- Pods:
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-sp2xc: Running (1/1)
  - web-app-deployment-5fd65c8bdc-zc9sf: Running (1/1)
- Service endpoints for web-app-service now list both pod IPs on port 80, so traffic will route correctly.

Why the error happened
- With no ready pods behind the Service, connecting to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 returned connection refused.

If you intended to pin these pods to special nodes
- Option A: Re-add a nodeSelector that matches real node labels (e.g., environment=production) after labeling the target node(s): kubectl label node <node> environment=production-gpu
- Option B: Use node affinity with fallbacks or taints/tolerations as appropriate.
- Let me know and I can reapply a placement policy that fits your environment.

Next steps I can do on request
- Add readiness/liveness probes for nginx to improve rollout safety.
- Create a quick test pod in the namespace to curl the Service and confirm end-to-end response content.
- Set resource requests/limits as needed.

For now, the deployment is fixed and serving through the Service.

results.taskOutput:
All requested objects have been created and applied to the cluster. Summary of what’s in place:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled:
  - dev-* and dev-shared: env=dev (dev-shared also shared=true)
  - staging: env=staging
  - prod: env=prod

2) RBAC
- Per-developer full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBinding in each dev namespace to ClusterRole admin for the respective user and service account:
    - dev-alice: alice + alice-sa
    - dev-bob: bob + bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: charlie + charlie-sa
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared to ClusterRole view for users alice, bob, charlie and SAs alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa
- Staging/prod restricted to cluster admins:
  - RoleBinding in staging and prod to ClusterRole admin for Group system:masters only
- Service accounts created:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny everywhere (ingress and egress) in all six namespaces
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow ingress only from same namespace
  - Allow egress to:
    - Same namespace
    - dev-shared (via namespace label shared=true)
    - DNS in kube-system (TCP/UDP 53; matches coredns/kube-dns pods)
- dev-shared:
  - Default deny
  - Allow ingress from namespaces labeled env=dev (all dev namespaces)
  - Allow egress to same namespace and DNS in kube-system
- staging/prod:
  - Default deny
  - Allow ingress only from same namespace
  - Allow egress only to DNS in kube-system
- Effect:
  - Cross-developer traffic is blocked
  - Dev namespaces can reach dev-shared but not each other, staging, or prod
  - Staging/prod are isolated from dev namespaces
  - All namespaces created here can resolve DNS

Notes on least privilege
- Developers and their service accounts are granted namespace-scoped admin within only their own namespaces, and view-only on dev-shared. No access to staging/prod unless in system:masters.
- The “view” role does not grant access to Secrets by default.
- If you prefer to restrict developers from managing RoleBindings in their own namespaces, use ClusterRole edit instead of admin. The requirement asked for “full access,” so admin was used.

How to use the developer service accounts (Kubernetes v1.24+)
- Get a short-lived token (default duration) for a service account:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa

Quick verification
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as bob
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice   # should be “no”
- Network:
  - From a test pod in dev-alice, curl a service/pod in dev-bob should fail
  - From a test pod in dev-alice, DNS queries should succeed
  - From a test pod in dev-alice, reaching a service/pod in dev-shared should succeed
  - From a test pod in staging, reaching dev namespaces should fail

Operational considerations
- Ensure your CNI enforces NetworkPolicy (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, Weave Net). If not, apply one.
- If your DNS pods in kube-system use different labels, adjust the DNS selectors in the policies.
- If pods need to reach external services (e.g., package registries), add targeted egress rules (by CIDR or FQDN if using a CNI that supports it).

If you want, I can export all applied manifests as a single bundle for GitOps or provide Helm/Kustomize overlays for repeatable environments.

Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All requested objects have been created and applied to the cluster. Summary of what’s in place:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled:
  - dev-* and dev-shared: env=dev (dev-shared also shared=true)
  - staging: env=staging
  - prod: env=prod

2) RBAC
- Per-developer full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBinding in each dev namespace to ClusterRole admin for the respective user and service account:
    - dev-alice: alice + alice-sa
    - dev-bob: bob + bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: charlie + charlie-sa
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared to ClusterRole view for users alice, bob, charlie and SAs alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa
- Staging/prod restricted to cluster admins:
  - RoleBinding in staging and prod to ClusterRole admin for Group system:masters only
- Service accounts created:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny everywhere (ingress and egress) in all six namespaces
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow ingress only from same namespace
  - Allow egress to:
    - Same namespace
    - dev-shared (via namespace label shared=true)
    - DNS in kube-system (TCP/UDP 53; matches coredns/kube-dns pods)
- dev-shared:
  - Default deny
  - Allow ingress from namespaces labeled env=dev (all dev namespaces)
  - Allow egress to same namespace and DNS in kube-system
- staging/prod:
  - Default deny
  - Allow ingress only from same namespace
  - Allow egress only to DNS in kube-system
- Effect:
  - Cross-developer traffic is blocked
  - Dev namespaces can reach dev-shared but not each other, staging, or prod
  - Staging/prod are isolated from dev namespaces
  - All namespaces created here can resolve DNS

Notes on least privilege
- Developers and their service accounts are granted namespace-scoped admin within only their own namespaces, and view-only on dev-shared. No access to staging/prod unless in system:masters.
- The “view” role does not grant access to Secrets by default.
- If you prefer to restrict developers from managing RoleBindings in their own namespaces, use ClusterRole edit instead of admin. The requirement asked for “full access,” so admin was used.

How to use the developer service accounts (Kubernetes v1.24+)
- Get a short-lived token (default duration) for a service account:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa

Quick verification
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as bob
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice   # should be “no”
- Network:
  - From a test pod in dev-alice, curl a service/pod in dev-bob should fail
  - From a test pod in dev-alice, DNS queries should succeed
  - From a test pod in dev-alice, reaching a service/pod in dev-shared should succeed
  - From a test pod in staging, reaching dev namespaces should fail

Operational considerations
- Ensure your CNI enforces NetworkPolicy (e.g., Calico, Cilium, Antrea, Weave Net). If not, apply one.
- If your DNS pods in kube-system use different labels, adjust the DNS selectors in the policies.
- If pods need to reach external services (e.g., package registries), add targeted egress rules (by CIDR or FQDN if using a CNI that supports it).

If you want, I can export all applied manifests as a single bundle for GitOps or provide Helm/Kustomize overlays for repeatable environments.

outputSteps.content:
All requested objects have been created and applied to the cluster. Summary of what’s in place:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labeled:
  - dev-* and dev-shared: env=dev (dev-shared also shared=true)
  - staging: env=staging
  - prod: env=prod

2) RBAC
- Per-developer full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBinding in each dev namespace to ClusterRole admin for the respective user and service account:
    - dev-alice: alice + alice-sa
    - dev-bob: bob + bob-sa
    - dev-charlie: charlie + charlie-sa
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared to ClusterRole view for users alice, bob, charlie and SAs alice-sa, bob-sa, charlie-sa
- Staging/prod restricted to cluster admins:
  - RoleBinding in staging and prod to ClusterRole admin for Group system:masters only
- Service accounts created:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2, requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi, pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - requests.cpu=4, limits.cpu=4, requests.memory=8Gi, limits.memory=8Gi, pods=20, services=10
- staging/prod:
  - requests.cpu=8, limits.cpu=8, requests.memory=16Gi, limits.memory=16Gi, pods=50, services=20

4) Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny everywhere (ingress and egress) in all six namespaces
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie):
  - Allow ingress only from same namespace
  - Allow egress to:
    - Same namespace
    - dev-shared (via namespace label shared=true)
    - DNS in kube-system (TCP/UDP 53; matches coredns/kube-dns pods)
- dev-shared:
  - Default deny
  - Allow ingress from namespaces labeled env=dev (all dev namespaces)
  - Allow egress to same namespace and DNS in kube-system
- staging/prod:
  - Default deny
  - Allow ingress only from same namespace
  - Allow egress only to DNS in kube-system
- Effect:
  - Cross-developer traffic is blocked
  - Dev namespaces can reach dev-shared but not each other, staging, or prod
  - Staging/prod are isolated from dev namespaces
  - All namespaces created here can resolve DNS

Notes on least privilege
- Developers and their service accounts are granted namespace-scoped admin within only their own namespaces, and view-only on dev-shared. No access to staging/prod unless in system:masters.
- The “view” role does not grant access to Secrets by default.
- If you prefer to restrict developers from managing RoleBindings in their own namespaces, use ClusterRole edit instead of admin. The requirement asked for “full access,” so admin was used.

How to use the developer service accounts (Kubernetes v1.24+)
- Get a short-lived token (default duration) for a service account:
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa

Quick verification
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as bob
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice   # should be “no”
- Network:
